issues.legal_issue: A public servant commits criminal misconduct by abusing official position to obtain a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for themselves or another person, and any one of the independent alternatives in the governing provision is sufficient.
material_facts: The appellant was the public authority’s chairperson-cum-chief executive officer and used her position to have a defective, undated application processed after the scheme’s closing date, despite an improper and late-cleared cheque.

She obtained conversion of her plot to a larger plot in a developed sector and approved a layout change that enlarged it further, made it a corner plot and reduced other land available to the authority.

Her two dependent daughters received shops and residential plots through defective applications and functional certificates; the evidence showed that the appellant and her husband funded the transactions and that the shops were used to obtain eligibility for residential plots.
The allotments and layout changes contravened the authority’s rules, gave valuable advantages to the appellant and her daughters, and caused loss to the authority.
The trial court and High Court convicted the appellant, and the Supreme Court found no error in their concurrent assessment of the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for criminal misconduct was confirmed because the appellant abused her public position to obtain valuable things or pecuniary advantages for herself and her daughters.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13(1)(d)(i), (ii) and (iii) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, the three alternatives are independent and disjunctive: obtaining a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage by corrupt or illegal means, by abusing public position, or for any person without public interest is sufficient to constitute criminal misconduct. Section 13(2) prescribes the punishment. The Court also referred to Manoj Narula v. Union of India (2014) 9 SCC 1, Niranjan Hemchandra Sashittal v. State of Maharashtra (2013) 4 SCC 642, Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh (2012) 3 SCC 64 and K.C. Sareen v. C.B.I. (2001) 6 SCC 584 in discussing the serious public harm caused by corruption; the elements applied to the conviction were those in Section 13(1)(d).

rule.if: appeal_against_corruption_conviction and public_servant and official_position_abused and valuable_advantage_obtained_for_self_or_another

predicates.appeal_against_corruption_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a conviction for corruption-related criminal misconduct.
predicates.public_servant: The accused held public office when the relevant conduct occurred.
predicates.official_position_abused: The public servant used the authority or influence of the office improperly in the relevant dealings.
predicates.valuable_advantage_obtained_for_self_or_: The public servant obtained a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for themselves or another person.

issues.definition: When a public servant’s abuse of office obtains a valuable advantage for the public servant or another person, an appeal against the resulting criminal-misconduct conviction may leave that conviction upheld.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent running of sentences imposed in separate cases arising from distinct transactions is discretionary and is not warranted merely because the same offender seeks it.
material_facts: The appellant sought concurrent running of imprisonment sentences imposed in two different cases.

One case concerned the appellant’s conduct in obtaining plots for herself and her daughters and making related layout changes; the other concerned a separate conspiracy to obtain a plot for another person.
The convictions were in separate cases and concerned different transactions.
The Court considered the nature and circumstances of the allegations and found no justification for concurrency.
issues.conclusion: The request for concurrent running of the sentences was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Section 427 CrPC governs a sentence imposed on an offender already sentenced for another offence and gives the court discretion to direct concurrency. That discretion must be exercised judicially in light of the totality of the circumstances; consecutive sentences are the normal approach, and concurrency is generally favoured for offences arising from a single transaction. Mohd. Akhtar Hussain v. Asst. Collector, Customs (1988) 4 SCC 183 states that the single-transaction principle does not apply when the transactions or facts are distinct. O.M. Cherian alias Thankachan v. State of Kerala (2015) 2 SCC 501, K. Prabhakaran v. P. Jayarajan (2005) 1 SCC 754, V.K. Bansal v. State of Haryana (2013) 7 SCC 211 and Benson v. State of Kerala (2016) 10 SCC 307 recognise the court’s discretion and the need to exercise it on the particular facts. Section 31 CrPC concerns multiple offences tried together; this case concerned sentences in separate cases and was governed by Section 427 CrPC.

predicates.request_for_concurrent_sentences: The offender asks the court to direct that imprisonment sentences run at the same time.
predicates.sentences_imposed_in_separate_cases: The imprisonment sentences were imposed in separate cases rather than for multiple offences at one trial.
predicates.sentences_arise_from_distinct_transactio: The conduct underlying the separate sentences involved distinct transactions.
predicates.no_special_circumstances_justify_concurr: The circumstances of the cases do not provide a particular reason to depart from consecutive sentences.

issues.definition: If an offender seeks concurrency for sentences imposed in separate cases arising from distinct transactions and no special circumstances support it, the request is refused.

issues.legal_issue: A court may reduce an imprisonment sentence in light of the circumstances surrounding the offender and the case.
material_facts: The appellant’s conviction was confirmed, but the imprisonment sentence was under consideration in the appeal.
The conduct had occurred many years earlier, and the appellant was undergoing the sentence.
The appellant’s husband stated by affidavit that the appellant had surrendered the plot and its building to the public authority and would make no claim for a refund.
The Court also noted that the appellant’s service and retirement benefits were in jeopardy as a result of the conviction.
issues.conclusion: The Court reduced the imprisonment sentence from three years to two years.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its sentencing discretion in light of the circumstances presented, including the passage of time, the surrender of the property and the consequences of the conviction for the appellant’s service and retirement benefits. No particular statutory provision or earlier case is identified in this part of the judgment as the basis for the reduction.

rule.if: sentence_under_review_in_criminal_appeal and long_time_since_conduct and property_surrendered and no_refund_claim_to_be_made and serious_service_consequences

predicates.sentence_under_review_in_criminal_appeal: An imprisonment sentence is being considered in a criminal appeal.
predicates.long_time_since_conduct: A substantial period has elapsed between the conduct and the sentencing decision under review.
predicates.property_surrendered: The offender surrendered property obtained through the conduct to the public authority.
predicates.no_refund_claim_to_be_made: The offender undertook not to seek repayment for the surrendered property.
predicates.serious_service_consequences: The conviction jeopardises the offender’s employment or retirement benefits.

issues.definition: When a sentence is under review in a criminal appeal and the conduct is long past, property has been surrendered without a claim for repayment, and the conviction has serious service consequences, the imprisonment sentence may be reduced.
